- When sentiment is strongly positive (e.g., >0.6) and forecast is below recent high, adjust upward to reflect bullish momentum.  
- When sentiment is negative (e.g., <0.3) and forecast is above recent high, adjust downward to reflect bearish pressure.  
- Avoid over-optimistic forecasts after sharp price spikes; reduce forecast peak by 5–10% to account for mean reversion.  
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed, favor mid-range forecasts with slight downward bias to hedge against volatility.  
- For 30-day horizons, if last 3–5 days show strong upward trend, forecast should not lag more than 1–2 days behind actual momentum.  
- If sentiment history shows repeated low values (e.g., <0.2) over 5+ days, apply a conservative downward bias to avoid overcorrection.  
- When sentiment spikes upward after a downtrend, forecast should accelerate upward but not exceed 20% above recent peak without validation.  
- If forecast consistently underestimates true price in 30-day window, increase baseline by 2–3% to account for lagged sentiment effects.
